title: Acute exposure to evening blue-enriched light impacts on human sleep
research_question: To investigate the impact of blue-enriched polychromatic light on human sleep architecture and sleep electroencephalographic activity.

participants.description: 30 healthy young participants (16 men, 14 women; age range 20-31 years, mean ± SD: 25.2 ± 3.1 years) from Switzerland. Non-smokers, not extreme chronotypes, free from medical, psychiatric, and sleep disorders, no visual impairments. Average sleep duration 7-8 h.
participants.recruitment: Participants gave written informed consent; screened by medical examination and questionnaires, and ophthalmologic examination.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 2 hours of evening light exposure to polychromatic light from compact fluorescent lamps or incandescent light bulb. Three conditions: 6500 K (blue-enriched), 2500 K (non-blue-enriched), and 3000 K (incandescent, broadband white light). Illumination levels set to 40 lux on a white wall, with light measure at eye level typically between 25 and 32 lux. Conditions were counterbalanced.

measures.instrument: Visually scored polysomnography (EEG, EOG, EMG) per Rechtschaffen and Kales (1968) criteria
Fast-Fourier transformation (FFT) of EEG data (0.50-20 Hz) during NREM and REM sleep, 8 derivations (F3, F4, C3, C4, P3, P4, O1, O2)
EEG power density in 2.0-4.0 Hz range, non-linear regression for decay function
% of total sleep time (TST) spent awake after lights off

findings.antecedent: Evening light exposure (6500 K vs 3000 K)
findings.mechanism: Blue-enriched light may have alerting effects that tend to reduce wakefulness during sleep.
findings.quote: less wakefulness during sleep following light exposure at 6500 K than light at 3000 K.

findings.antecedent: Interaction of evening light exposure (6500 K vs 3000 K) and sleep cycle
findings.consequent: NREM sleep Stage 1 (% of Total Sleep Time)
findings.mechanism: Blue-enriched light may alter the progression of sleep stages, particularly in the first sleep cycle.
findings.quote: more NREM sleep Stage 1 following light at 6500 K than at 3000 K, during the first NREM-REM sleep cycle

findings.antecedent: Interaction of evening light condition and EEG derivation
findings.consequent: All-night NREM sleep EEG power density (1.75-3.25 Hz)
findings.mechanism: Light's effect on NREM EEG power density may vary across brain regions.
findings.quote: a tendency for the interaction of factors 'light condition' and 'derivation' in the frequency bins of 1.75-3.25 Hz (F6,168 > 2.5; P < 0.1).

findings.antecedent: Evening light condition (6500 K, 2500 K, 3000 K)
findings.consequent: All-night NREM sleep EEG power density (0.50-20 Hz)
findings.mechanism: Overall light condition did not significantly impact all-night NREM EEG power density.
findings.quote: The main factor 'light condition' revealed no significance

findings.consequent: All-night NREM sleep EEG power density
findings.mechanism: EEG power density varies across different brain regions.
findings.quote: the main factor 'derivation' yielded significance in the frequency ranges of 0.50-5.0 Hz, 6.75-7.75 Hz, 9.25-12.0 Hz and 13.0-15.5 Hz (F3,84 > 3.6; P < 0.05).

findings.antecedent: Evening light exposure (6500 K vs 2500 K and 3000 K)
findings.consequent: Frontal NREM EEG power density (1.75-3.25 Hz)
findings.mechanism: Blue-enriched light tends to reduce frontal NREM EEG power density.
findings.quote: Exposure to light at 6500 K resulted in a tendency for less frontal NREM EEG power density in the range of 1.75-3.25 Hz, in comparison to light at 2500 K and 3000 K (P < 0.1; Tukey-Kramer test).

findings.antecedent: Evening light condition (6500 K, 2500 K, 3000 K)
findings.consequent: All-night REM sleep EEG power density
findings.mechanism: Light condition did not significantly impact REM sleep EEG power density.
findings.quote: All-night REM sleep EEG power density did not differ significantly across the three light conditions (data not shown).

findings.antecedent: Evening light exposure (6500 K vs 2500 K and 3000 K)
findings.consequent: NREM EEG power density (2.25-4.25 Hz) per sleep cycle
findings.mechanism: Blue-enriched light reduces NREM EEG activity in specific frequency bins across sleep cycles.
findings.quote: light at 6500 K resulting in less EEG activity in these frequency bins, compared to light at 3000 K and 2500 K.

findings.antecedent: Interaction of evening light condition and sleep cycle
findings.consequent: NREM EEG power density (2.0-4.0 Hz) per derivation
findings.mechanism: The effect of light on NREM EEG power density varies across sleep cycles and derivations.
findings.quote: A two-way ANOVA with the interaction of factors 'light condition' and 'cycle', for each derivation separately, elicited significant differences in the frequency bins from 2.0 to 4.0 Hz (F4,86 > 1.2; P < 0.05).

findings.antecedent: Evening light exposure (6500 K vs 2500 K and 3000 K)
findings.consequent: NREM EEG power density (SWA 2.0-4.0 Hz) during the first NREM-REM sleep cycle
findings.mechanism: Blue-enriched light acutely reduces slow wave activity in the initial sleep period, impacting homeostatic sleep regulation.
findings.quote: light at 6500 K resulted in less EEG power density in the frequency range from 2.0 to 4.0 Hz (SWA range), relative to light at 3000 K and 2500 K (P < 0.05; Tukey-Kramer test).

findings.antecedent: Interaction of evening light condition and percentiles during NREM sleep cycles
findings.mechanism: The dynamics of frontal SWA across sleep cycles are modulated by light exposure.
findings.quote: a significant interaction for only the frontal derivation (F18,265 = 1.86; P = 0.04).

findings.consequent: Frontal NREM SWA (2.0-4.0 Hz) during the first sleep cycle (time intervals 4-8)
findings.mechanism: Blue-enriched light significantly reduces frontal SWA during the early part of the first sleep cycle.
findings.quote: significantly less frontal NREM SWA during the first sleep cycle [time intervals 4-8 (percentiles) during NREM sleep)] following exposure to light at 6500 K (P < 0.05; Tukey-Kramer test) (Fig. 1).

findings.antecedent: Evening light condition (6500 K, 2500 K, 3000 K)
findings.mechanism: Light condition did not significantly affect the rate at which SWA dissipates across the night.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA performed on the rate of SWA dissipation across the three light conditions (for each derivation separately) revealed no significant differences.

findings.antecedent: Evening light exposure (6500 K vs 3000 K)
findings.consequent: Predicted amount of frontal SWA (derived from non-linear exponential function)
findings.mechanism: Blue-enriched light reduces the overall predicted amount of frontal SWA.
findings.quote: less SWA following light at 6500 K compared to light at 3000 K, for only the frontal derivation.

findings.consequent: Predicted amount of frontal SWA (derived from non-linear exponential function)
findings.mechanism: SWA naturally decreases across sleep cycles.

findings.antecedent: Interaction of evening light condition and sleep cycle
findings.consequent: Predicted amount of frontal SWA (derived from non-linear exponential function)
findings.mechanism: The interaction between light condition and sleep cycle did not significantly affect the predicted amount of frontal SWA.
findings.quote: The interaction of these factors did not yield significance.

mechanisms: Blue-enriched light may elicit a stronger wake-promoting signal onto the SCN and VLPO, shifting the balance of inhibitory interaction towards sleep promotion and arousal inhibition.

Blue-enriched light may counteract the increased susceptibility of the frontal cortex to higher sleep pressure/neuronal tiredness due to use-dependent factors, leading to less frontal NREM SWA at the beginning of sleep.
Effects are mediated by non-image-forming photoreceptors, likely melanopsin-based photoreception.
implementation_implications: Exposure to blue-enriched polychromatic light at relatively low room light levels impacts upon homeostatic sleep regulation.
Commercially available compact fluorescent lights with different colour temperatures may impact significantly upon circadian physiology and sleep.

tables.description: Intensity and spectral composition of the polychromatic light settings (6500 K, 3000 K, 2500 K) including illuminance, correlated colour temperature, photon density, irradiance, and melanopic-weighted values.
Visually scored sleep stages subsequent to light exposure at 6500 K, 3000 K and 2500 K (n = 30), including TST, sleep efficiency, wake, and percentages of different sleep stages, and sleep latencies.

limitations: Absence of a control night (no light pulses) makes the full extent of light effects on sleep structure and EEG power density unclear.
The study tested acute effects, not allowing for assessment of long-term effects of chronic light exposure.
Prior light exposure history was controlled stringently, but individual prior light history was not controlled, so effects of individual prior light history cannot be ruled out.
Generalizing results to real-life conditions should be done with caution due to stringent control for 'photic memory'.

paper_metadata.title: Acute exposure to evening blue‐enriched light impacts on human sleep
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Acute exposure to evening blue‐enriched light impacts on human sleep
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: SummaryLight in the short wavelength range (blue light: 446–483 nm) elicits direct effects on human melatonin secretion, alertness and cognitive performance via non‐image‐forming photoreceptors. However, the impact of blue‐enriched polychromatic light on human sleep architecture and sleep electroencephalographic activity remains fairly unknown. In this study we investigated sleep structure and sleep electroencephalographic characteristics of 30 healthy young participants (16 men, 14 women; age range 20–31 years) following 2 h of evening light exposure to polychromatic light at 6500 K, 2500 K and 3000 K. Sleep structure across the first three non‐rapid eye movement non‐rapid eye movement – rapid eye movement sleep cycles did not differ significantly with respect to the light conditions. All‐night non‐rapid eye movement sleep electroencephalographic power density indicated that exposure to light at 6500 K resulted in a tendency for less frontal non‐rapid eye movement electroencephalographic power density, compared to light at 2500 K and 3000 K. The dynamics of non‐rapid eye movement electroencephalographic slow wave activity (2.0–4.0 Hz), a functional index of homeostatic sleep pressure, were such that slow wave activity was reduced significantly during the first sleep cycle after light at 6500 K compared to light at 2500 K and 3000 K, particularly in the frontal derivation. Our data suggest that exposure to blue‐enriched polychromatic light at relatively low room light levels impacts upon homeostatic sleep regulation, as indexed by reduction in frontal slow wave activity during the first non‐rapid eye movement episode.

environmental_features: blue-enriched light (6500 K, ~250 lux at eye level)
standard warm white light (3000 K, ~250 lux at eye level)
stimulus_description.duration_exposure: 2 hours in the evening before bedtime

mechanism_chain.description: Evening exposure to blue-enriched light activates intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs), which signal to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN). This signaling leads to the suppression of melatonin production and an increase in alertness, ultimately impacting sleep onset and architecture, such as increasing wakefulness.

steps.to_construct: Activation of intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs)
Suppression of melatonin production and increased alertness

instruments_used.name: Polysomnography (PSG)
instruments_used.construct: sleep architecture, sleep stages (NREM, REM), wakefulness, sleep latency
instruments_used.description: Objective measurement of brain waves (EEG), eye movements (EOG), and muscle activity (EMG) during sleep

instruments_used.name: Spectroradiometer
instruments_used.description: Device used to measure the spectral composition and intensity of the light stimuli

instruments_used.name: Salivary Melatonin Assay
instruments_used.description: Measurement of melatonin concentration in saliva samples

instruments_used.name: Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS)
instruments_used.description: 9-point self-report scale measuring current level of sleepiness
